passages.title: Hannah prays and dedicates Samuel
passages.summary: Elkanah has two wives, and Hannah has no children. Each year at Shiloh the other wife taunts her until she weeps. Hannah prays in bitter grief and vows to give a son to the LORD. Eli the priest sees her lips move and thinks she is drunk. She explains, and he sends her away with a blessing. She bears a son and names him Samuel. When he is weaned she brings him to Eli at Shiloh. She gives him to the LORD for his whole life.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies Hannah's prayer during grief and her trust in God. How does Hannah answer Eli in verses 15–16?

contextNote.title: A suffering woman's voice corrects a priest
contextNote.text: Three people misread Hannah in this chapter. Her rival provokes her (verse 6). Her husband asks if he is not better than ten sons (verse 8). The priest takes her silent prayer for drunkenness (verses 13–14). In verses 15–16 she corrects him firmly and with respect. Eli changes his charge into a blessing (verse 17). Verse 18 says her face was no longer sad, before any child is born.

passages.title: Hannah’s song and the failure of Eli’s sons
passages.summary: Hannah sings that the LORD brings down the strong and lifts the poor. Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are priests who do not know the LORD. They take the best meat by force before the fat is burned. They also sleep with women who serve at the tent door. Eli rebukes them, but they do not listen. Meanwhile the boy Samuel grows and serves before the LORD. A man of God tells Eli that his house will lose the priesthood. Both sons will die on one day.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects Hannah's song with Jesus Christ. What does the man of God say Eli has honored above the LORD (verse 29)?

contextNote.title: The household tests the meaning of sacred office
contextNote.text: The sons’ sin is plain in verses 13–17 and 22. Eli’s part is harder to see. He does speak to them (verses 23–25), but with words only. Verse 29 charges him with honoring his sons above God. It also says “yourselves,” so he shares in what they took. Verse 30 states the rule that follows: the LORD honors those who honor him. Between these scenes the text keeps noting Samuel’s growth (verses 18, 21, 26).

passages.title: Samuel hears the call
passages.summary: The boy Samuel serves under Eli, and words from the LORD are rare. One night a voice calls Samuel, and he runs to Eli. This happens three times before Eli understands. He tells Samuel to answer, “Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.” The LORD says he will judge Eli’s house for the sons’ sin. Eli knew and did not restrain them. In the morning Samuel is afraid, but Eli makes him tell everything. All Israel learns that Samuel is a prophet.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Samuel’s response with learning to recognize revelation. Who teaches Samuel how to answer the voice (verses 8–9)?

contextNote.title: Receiving a call includes speaking difficult words
contextNote.text: Samuel’s first message is a judgment on the man who raised him. Verse 15 says he was afraid to tell it. Eli himself taught the boy how to listen (verse 9). Eli also insists on hearing every word (verse 17). In verse 18 Samuel hides nothing, and Eli accepts the sentence. The text does not report that he changed anything afterward. Verse 19 says the LORD let none of Samuel’s words fail.

passages.title: The ark is captured and Eli’s household suffers loss
passages.summary: Israel fights the Philistines and loses four thousand men. The elders send to Shiloh for the ark of the covenant. Hophni and Phinehas come with it, and the camp shouts. The Philistines are afraid but urge each other to fight like men. Israel loses thirty thousand men, the ark is captured, and Eli’s sons die. A runner brings the news to Shiloh. Eli falls from his seat and dies when he hears about the ark. His daughter-in-law dies in childbirth and names her son Ichabod.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson examines trust in the ark. Why does carrying the ark fail to protect the army?

contextNote.title: A sacred object cannot secure a chosen outcome
contextNote.text: The elders ask a good question in verse 3: why did the LORD defeat us? They do not wait for an answer. They send for the ark so that “it” may save them. The priests who come with it are the two condemned in 2:34. The shout in verse 5 is confident, and the loss is far worse. Chapter 7:3–4 later shows what was missing here. The people had not put away their other gods.

passages.title: The ark among the Philistine towns
passages.summary: The Philistines bring the ark to Ashdod and set it beside their god Dagon. The next morning Dagon’s statue lies face down before the ark. They set it up, and the next day it has fallen again. Its head and hands lie broken on the threshold. The LORD strikes Ashdod with tumors. The people send the ark to Gath, and the same thing happens. Gath sends it to Ekron, and Ekron cries out in terror. The city’s cry goes up to heaven.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older manual connects the ark’s troubles with Israel’s need to honor God. What do the men of Ashdod conclude in verse 7?

contextNote.title: Power is questioned outside Israel's territory
contextNote.text: The Philistines won the battle and placed the ark as a trophy (verse 2). No Israelite soldier or priest is present in this chapter. The LORD acts alone in the enemy’s own temple. In verse 7 the men of Ashdod read the events correctly. His hand is heavy on them and on Dagon. Their answer is to send the problem to the next town (verse 8). Each move spreads the harm (verses 9–12).

passages.title: The ark returns to Beth Shemesh
passages.summary: After seven months the Philistines ask their priests how to send the ark back. The priests advise a guilt offering of five golden tumors and five golden mice. They warn the people not to harden their hearts as Egypt did. They hitch two milk cows to a new cart and pen up the calves. If the cows go toward Israel, the LORD sent the plague. The cows walk straight to Beth Shemesh, lowing as they go. The people there rejoice and offer the cows. Some look into the ark and die, and the town sends it away.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson uses these events to study trust and obedience. Why do the Philistines use cows that have calves at home (verses 7–9)?

contextNote.title: The return includes a stated test of cause
contextNote.text: The Philistine priests design a test in verses 7–9. Nursing cows that never pulled a cart should turn back to their calves. If they leave, something stronger than instinct is moving them. Verse 9 names the other option honestly: it may have been chance. Verse 12 reports the result, with the cows lowing all the way. The ark is no safer for Israel’s own town (verse 19). Beth Shemesh asks who can stand before this holy God (verse 20).

passages.title: Samuel leads the gathering at Mizpah
passages.summary: The ark stays at Kiriath Jearim for twenty years. Samuel tells Israel to put away foreign gods and serve the LORD alone. They do so and gather at Mizpah to fast and confess. The Philistines hear of the gathering and attack. The people beg Samuel to keep praying for them. He offers a lamb, and the LORD thunders against the Philistines. Israel chases them, and Samuel sets up a stone named Ebenezer. Samuel judges Israel on a yearly circuit from his home in Ramah.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies turning toward God after earlier failure. What does Israel do in verses 3–6 before the battle?

contextNote.title: A victory becomes a named act of remembrance
contextNote.text: The name Ebenezer first appears in 4:1, where Israel camped before defeat. There the people fetched the ark and shouted. Here they put away their gods and confess (verses 4 and 6). They ask Samuel to pray; they do not ask for an object (verse 8). The same enemy is driven back. In verse 12 Samuel marks the place with a stone and a name. His words are modest: the LORD has helped “until now.”

passages.title: The people request a king
passages.summary: Samuel grows old, and his sons take bribes as judges. The elders ask him for a king like all the nations have. Samuel is displeased and prays. The LORD says the people have rejected him, not Samuel, as king. Samuel must warn them how a king will behave. A king will take their sons, daughters, fields, crops, servants, and flocks. They will cry out, and the LORD will not answer. The people still insist, and the LORD tells Samuel to give them a king.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson invites readers to consider Jesus Christ as their King. What does verse 17 say the people will become under a king?

contextNote.title: A king can take what a people needs
contextNote.text: The elders have a real complaint: Samuel’s sons are corrupt (verse 3). Their fix is to be “like all the nations” (verse 5). Samuel’s warning repeats one phrase again and again: “he will take.” The list runs from sons and daughters to fields and flocks (verses 11–17). Verse 17 ends it: “you will be his servants.” The LORD once brought Israel out of service to a king in Egypt. The people hear all this and still choose it (verses 19–20).

passages.title: Saul searches for donkeys and meets Samuel
passages.summary: Saul, a tall young man of Benjamin, searches for his father’s lost donkeys. After three days he wants to turn back. His servant suggests asking a man of God in the nearby town. The servant also supplies the silver for a gift. The day before, the LORD told Samuel that a Benjamite would come. Samuel must anoint him as leader over Israel. Samuel seats Saul at the head of a feast and gives him a reserved portion. Saul says his tribe is the smallest and his family the least.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Saul’s selection with a call to service. Who suggests visiting the man of God in verse 6?

contextNote.title: A servant opens the way to royal appointment
contextNote.text: Saul is about to give up the search in verse 5. The unnamed servant knows about the man of God (verse 6). The servant also has the quarter shekel (verse 8). Saul does not even recognize Samuel at the gate (verse 18). Verses 15–16 show the other side of the story. The LORD had already told Samuel when the man would come. Lost donkeys and a servant’s idea bring Saul to that meeting.

passages.title: Saul is anointed and presented publicly
passages.summary: Samuel pours oil on Saul’s head and names three signs for the road home. All three happen, and God gives Saul another heart. The Spirit comes on him, and he prophesies among a band of prophets. He tells his uncle about the donkeys but not about the kingdom. Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah and chooses by lot. The lot falls on Saul, who is hiding among the baggage. The people shout, “Long live the king!” Some men despise him, and he keeps silent.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson connects anointing and changed purpose with service by revelation. Where is Saul when the lot names him (verse 22)?

contextNote.title: Public selection does not erase uncertainty
contextNote.text: Saul already has the oil, the signs, and a changed heart (verses 1–9). When the lot falls on him, he cannot be found. The people must ask the LORD where he is (verse 22). The text gives no reason for his hiding. It may be modesty or fear, and the chapter leaves that open. Samuel presents him by his height (verses 23–24). In verse 19 Samuel has just said that Israel rejected God that day.

passages.title: Saul relieves Jabesh Gilead
passages.summary: Nahash the Ammonite surrounds Jabesh Gilead. He will make peace only if he may put out every right eye. The town sends messengers through Israel. Saul comes in from the field behind his oxen and hears the news. God’s Spirit comes on him, and he is very angry. He cuts up the oxen and sends the pieces as a summons. Israel gathers, and Saul breaks the Ammonite camp at dawn. He refuses to punish his critics, and the people renew the kingdom at Gilgal.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older manual studies Saul’s early leadership and the renewed kingdom. How does Saul answer the call for executions in verse 13?

contextNote.title: Victory gives Saul a chance to restrain revenge
contextNote.text: In 10:27 some men asked how Saul could save them. After the victory the people want those men put to death (verse 12). Saul now has the power and the public support to do it. Verse 13 records his refusal. He gives the credit for the rescue to the LORD, not to himself. This is Saul at his best: moved by the Spirit and restrained in victory. Later chapters should be read against this one.

passages.title: Samuel reviews leadership and covenant responsibility
passages.summary: Samuel speaks to all Israel now that a king leads them. He asks whom he has cheated, oppressed, or taken a bribe from. The people answer that he has taken nothing. He reviews how the LORD rescued them each time they cried out. Still they asked for a king when the LORD was their king. If they and their king obey, it will go well. Samuel calls for thunder and rain at wheat harvest, and the people are afraid. He promises to keep praying for them and teaching them.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older manual studies Samuel’s final address and continued prayer for the people. What does Samuel ask the people to testify in verse 3?

contextNote.title: The outgoing leader invites public examination
contextNote.text: In 8:11–17 Samuel warned that a king would “take.” In verse 3 he asks whose ox or donkey he himself has taken. The people clear him before the LORD and the new king (verses 4–5). His clean record becomes the standard the king will be measured by. Verses 14–15 place king and people under the same condition. Samuel gives up rule but not his work. Verse 23 says he would sin if he stopped praying for them.

passages.title: Pressure at Michmash and Saul’s offering
passages.summary: Jonathan attacks a Philistine post, and the Philistines gather a huge army. Israel’s men hide in caves and pits, and some cross the Jordan. Saul waits seven days at Gilgal for Samuel, as he was told. Samuel does not come, and the soldiers begin to leave. Saul offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives at once and says Saul’s kingdom will not last. The LORD has sought a man after his own heart. Saul is left with six hundred men, and only he and Jonathan have swords.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 1 Samuel names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies obedience under pressure. The older manual also reads the offering as unauthorized priesthood action. What three reasons does Saul give in verses 11–12?

contextNote.title: Pressure reveals competing accounts of responsibility
contextNote.text: Saul’s answer in verse 11 lists three things he saw. The people were scattering, Samuel was late, and the Philistines had gathered. Verses 5–8 confirm that all three were true. His conclusion follows in verse 12: “I forced myself.” Every reason concerns what he could see. None concerns the instruction in 10:8 to wait. Samuel’s reply in verse 13 names only that: Saul did not keep the command.

passages.title: Jonathan’s attack and Saul’s dangerous oath
passages.summary: Jonathan and his armor bearer climb to a Philistine post alone. Jonathan says the LORD can save by many or by few. They kill about twenty men, and panic spreads through the Philistine camp. Saul joins the fight and puts a curse on anyone who eats before evening. Jonathan has not heard it and eats some honey. The hungry soldiers later eat meat with the blood. God gives Saul no answer, and the lot falls on Jonathan. Saul says he must die, but the people rescue him.

lds.text: The older manual studies Jonathan’s faith and the harmful effect of Saul’s oath. Why do the people refuse to let Jonathan die (verse 45)?

contextNote.title: The people challenge a royal sentence
contextNote.text: Saul’s oath in verse 24 speaks of “my enemies.” It weakens his own army on the day of victory. Jonathan says so plainly in verse 29: his father has troubled the land. The hunger leads the soldiers to break the law about blood (verse 32). Saul then swears twice more that the guilty will die (verses 39 and 44). In verse 45 the people overrule their king. They say Jonathan worked “with God” that day.

passages.title: Amalek, Agag, and Saul’s rejection
passages.summary: Samuel gives Saul the LORD’s command to destroy Amalek completely. The reason given is Amalek’s attack on Israel after Egypt. Saul defeats them but spares King Agag and the best animals. The LORD tells Samuel he regrets making Saul king. Saul greets Samuel and claims he has obeyed. Samuel asks about the sheep he hears and says obeying is better than sacrifice. Saul admits he feared the people, and the LORD rejects him as king. Samuel kills Agag and never visits Saul again.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks why obedience matters more than making a religious display. Whom does Saul blame in verse 21, and what purpose does he claim?

contextNote.title: Claiming a sacred purpose does not end the dispute
contextNote.text: Saul’s account changes as Samuel presses him. In verse 13 he says he has done what the LORD commanded. In verse 15 “they” spared the animals, for sacrifice. In verses 20–21 he obeyed, but “the people” took the plunder. Verse 9 had said that Saul and the people spared them together. He speaks of “the LORD your God” three times (verses 15, 21, 30). In verse 30 he still asks to be honored before the elders.

passages.title: David is anointed and enters Saul’s service
passages.summary: The LORD sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a son of Jesse. Samuel admires the eldest, but the LORD looks at the heart. Seven sons pass by, and none is chosen. The youngest, David, is brought from the sheep, and Samuel anoints him. The LORD’s Spirit comes on David and leaves Saul. A troubling spirit torments Saul, and his servants seek a harp player. One of them recommends David. David enters Saul’s service, and his music gives the king relief.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson asks readers to consider a person's heart instead of outward appearance. What does David’s music do for Saul in verse 23?

contextNote.title: Music belongs inside the court
contextNote.text: In verses 13–14 the Spirit comes on David and leaves Saul. Saul’s own servants then bring the newly anointed man to court (verse 18). Saul loves him and makes him armor bearer (verse 21). He does not know what Samuel did in Bethlehem. David’s first service to the king is to ease him, not replace him. He plays a harp (verse 23); the Egyptian harp shown is only a comparison. The text says the troubling spirit was “from God” and explains no more.

passages.title: David faces Goliath in the Valley of Elah
passages.summary: The Philistine champion Goliath challenges Israel to single combat for forty days. Saul and his army are afraid. David brings food to his brothers and hears the challenge. He tells Saul that the LORD saved him from a lion and a bear. Saul dresses David in his own armor, but David takes it off. He chooses five smooth stones and his sling. He tells Goliath that the battle is the LORD’s. One stone sinks into the giant’s forehead, and David cuts off his head.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how trust in God can give courage during a hard task. Why does David take off Saul’s armor (verse 39)?

contextNote.title: The chosen tools change the contest
contextNote.text: Verses 5–7 list Goliath’s armor and weapons piece by piece. Saul answers in kind in verse 38 with a helmet and coat of mail. Saul is Israel’s tallest man (9:2) and its king, yet he stays back. David says he cannot go in gear he has not tested (verse 39). In verse 40 he takes a shepherd’s tools. His speech in verses 45–47 gives the reason. The LORD does not save by sword and spear.

passages.title: Friendship, jealousy, and royal marriage plans
passages.summary: Jonathan loves David and makes a covenant with him. He gives David his own robe, sword, and bow. Women sing that Saul has killed thousands and David ten thousands. Saul becomes angry and watches David from that day. Twice he throws a spear at him. He offers his daughter Merab, then gives her to another man. Michal loves David, and Saul asks a deadly bride price, hoping the Philistines kill him. David pays double, and Saul fears him even more.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson compares Jonathan’s support with Saul’s jealousy. What does Saul conclude from the women’s song in verse 8?

contextNote.title: Public praise turns achievement into a royal threat
contextNote.text: The song praises Saul too, but he hears only the comparison. In verse 8 he leaps from a song to the loss of his kingdom. Jonathan is the heir and has the most to lose. Yet in verse 4 he hands David his robe and weapons. The chapter repeats that the LORD was with David (verses 12, 14, 28). It also repeats that Saul was afraid (verses 12, 15, 29). Each plan to harm David ends by raising him higher.

passages.title: Michal helps David escape
passages.summary: Saul tells Jonathan and his servants to kill David. Jonathan defends David, and Saul swears he will not die. War returns, David wins again, and Saul throws his spear a third time. Saul’s men watch David’s house that night. Michal lowers David from a window and puts a household idol in his bed. David flees to Samuel at Ramah. Three groups of Saul’s messengers are overcome and begin to prophesy. Saul goes himself, and the Spirit overcomes him too.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older Church manual compares Samuel's group of prophets with later Church schools. How does Michal answer her father in verse 17?

contextNote.title: A daughter acts against her father's violence
contextNote.text: Both of Saul’s children protect David against him. Jonathan does it by argument (verses 4–5). Michal does it by a trick (verses 11–16). In verse 17 Saul calls her husband “my enemy.” Michal shields herself with a lie, and the text does not comment. Saul’s oath in verse 6 lasts only until the next spear (verse 10). In verses 23–24 the Spirit stops him when nothing else has.

passages.title: Jonathan warns David and renews their covenant
passages.summary: David asks Jonathan why Saul wants him dead. They agree on a test at the new moon feast. Jonathan asks David to show kindness to his family in the future. At the feast Saul notices David’s empty seat. He rages at Jonathan and says David blocks his way to the throne. Jonathan asks what David has done, and Saul throws a spear at him. Jonathan warns David with a signal of arrows in the field. They weep, swear friendship again, and part.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: What does Jonathan risk by protecting David from his father?

contextNote.title: Succession makes friendship politically costly
contextNote.text: Saul states the matter plainly in verse 31. While David lives, Jonathan will not be king. On the facts Saul is right, and Jonathan already knows it. In verses 14–15 he asks David to spare his family later. He speaks as if David’s rule is certain. His answer to his father in verse 32 is about justice. Saul’s reply is a spear thrown at his own son (verse 33).

passages.title: David seeks food at Nob and refuge at Gath
passages.summary: David flees alone to the priests at Nob. He tells Ahimelech that the king sent him on secret business. He asks for bread, and the priest has only the holy bread. Ahimelech gives it once he hears the men have kept from women. David also takes Goliath’s sword, which was kept there. Doeg the Edomite, Saul’s chief herdsman, is present that day. David goes on to King Achish of Gath, where the servants recognize him. He pretends to be mad, and Achish sends him away.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older manual connects the bread account with Jesus’s later teaching about human need. What bread does the priest give David in verse 6?

contextNote.title: Need tests the use of sacred food
contextNote.text: Leviticus 24:5–9 reserves this bread for the priests. Ahimelech asks one question about the men’s condition (verse 4). Then he gives the bread, and verse 6 explains that no other was there. The text treats a hungry man’s need as reason enough. Jesus later cites this meal in Matthew 12:3–4. David gained the bread with a false story (verse 2). Verse 7 notes who was watching, and chapter 22 shows the cost.

passages.title: David gathers followers and Saul orders the Nob massacre
passages.summary: David hides in the cave of Adullam. His family and about four hundred troubled men join him. He leaves his parents with the king of Moab. Saul complains that his servants conspire against him. Doeg reports that Ahimelech gave David food and a sword. Ahimelech says David was the king’s loyal son-in-law. Saul orders the priests killed, and only Doeg obeys. Eighty-five priests and the town of Nob die, and Abiathar escapes to David.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older Church manual condemns Saul's attack on the priests. How do Saul’s guards respond to his order in verse 17?

contextNote.title: Royal command does not make every action acceptable
contextNote.text: Saul’s order in verse 17 names the victims as “priests of the LORD.” His own guards hear those words and will not strike. Their refusal is silent, and the text records no punishment. Doeg, a foreigner, does what Israelites refuse to do (verse 18). Verse 19 lists men, women, children, and animals. Saul spared such things in Amalek against a command (15:9). David admits in verse 22 that his visit caused these deaths.

passages.title: Keilah, wilderness pursuit, and Jonathan’s support
passages.summary: David asks the LORD twice and then rescues the town of Keilah from Philistines. Saul hears and prepares to trap him inside its gates. David asks through the priest’s ephod whether Keilah will hand him over. The answer is yes, so he leaves with six hundred men. Jonathan finds him in the wilderness and strengthens his trust in God. The people of Ziph tell Saul where David hides. Saul closes in around a mountain. A Philistine raid calls him away just in time.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: How does David respond when the town he saved may hand him over?

contextNote.title: Rescue does not guarantee political loyalty
contextNote.text: David has just saved Keilah from its enemies (verse 5). Verse 12 says the town would still give him to Saul. The text gives no reason. The fate of Nob in 22:19 was recent, and Keilah had walls to lose. David does not punish or argue; he leaves (verse 13). Saul assumes God has handed David to him (verse 7). David asks instead of assuming, and the answer keeps him alive.

passages.title: David spares Saul in the cave
passages.summary: Saul takes three thousand men to hunt David at En Gedi. He enters a cave alone, and David’s men are hiding deep inside. They say the LORD has given David his enemy. David cuts off a corner of Saul’s robe and then regrets even that. He will not harm the LORD’s anointed. Outside, he bows and shows Saul the cloth. Saul weeps and says David is more righteous than he is. He admits David will be king and asks mercy for his family.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites readers to study David's self-control and forgiveness. What does David hold up as proof in verse 11?

contextNote.title: Restraint supplies evidence against an accusation
contextNote.text: David’s men and David read the same chance in opposite ways. They see a gift from God (verse 4). He sees a king whom God anointed (verse 6). In verse 11 the piece of robe serves as evidence. He could have killed, and the cloth shows he chose not to. He calls Saul “my father” and leaves judgment to the LORD (verse 12). Saul agrees with every word, yet verse 22 has them go separate ways.

passages.title: Abigail prevents David’s revenge
passages.summary: Samuel dies, and Israel mourns him. David’s men have guarded the flocks of Nabal, a rich and harsh man. David asks for food at shearing time, and Nabal insults him. David arms four hundred men and swears to kill every male. Nabal’s wife Abigail hurries out with food and meets David on the road. She asks him not to shed blood he will later regret. David blesses her and turns back. Nabal dies ten days later, and David marries Abigail.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies restraint and forgiveness. It compares Abigail’s intervention with Jesus Christ. What does David thank Abigail for in verse 33?

contextNote.title: Wisdom stops violence before it gains praise
contextNote.text: In chapter 24 David spared a king who hunted him. Here an insult is enough to send him out with swords (verses 21–22). Abigail acts without telling her husband (verse 19). Her case in verses 30–31 looks ahead to David’s rule. A future king should not carry needless bloodshed on his conscience. In verse 33 David admits she stopped him from avenging himself. He credits the LORD with sending her (verse 32).

passages.title: David takes the spear and water jar
passages.summary: The people of Ziph again tell Saul where David is. Saul camps with three thousand men. David and Abishai slip into the camp at night and find Saul asleep. Abishai offers to pin him to the ground with one stroke. David forbids it and takes Saul’s spear and water jar. From a far hill he calls to Abner and to Saul. Saul admits he has played the fool and promises no more harm. David returns the spear, and each goes his own way.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies self-control. Restraint and continued separation occur together in the story. What does David tell Abner to look for in verse 16?

contextNote.title: A second refusal also questions royal protection
contextNote.text: David’s words in verse 16 are aimed at Abner, the king’s guard. The missing spear and jar prove how close death came. Saul threw that spear at David in 18:11 and 19:10. David has it in his hand and sends it back (verse 22). His reason is in verses 10–11: the LORD will deal with Saul. Saul’s blessing in verse 25 sounds like peace. In 27:1 David still expects Saul to kill him.

passages.title: David lives under Achish and conceals his raids
passages.summary: David decides that Saul will one day kill him. He crosses to the Philistines with six hundred men and their families. King Achish of Gath gives him the town of Ziklag. Saul stops searching for him. David raids the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites to the south. He leaves no one alive and takes the livestock. He tells Achish that he has raided Judah. Achish believes David’s own people now hate him.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older manual links David’s raids with earlier commands to take the land. The raids also kill whole households. What reason does verse 11 give for the killing?

contextNote.title: Safety under a patron depends on concealed violence
contextNote.text: Verse 11 states David’s reason in plain terms. He leaves no one alive who could report to Gath. The chapter does not say the LORD ordered these raids. David asked the LORD before acting in 23:2 and 23:4. No such question appears here. His safety with Achish rests on a lie (verse 10). Verse 12 shows that Achish is fully deceived.

passages.title: Saul consults the woman at Endor
passages.summary: The Philistines gather for war, and Achish expects David to fight for him. Samuel is dead, and Saul has driven mediums from the land. Saul is afraid, and the LORD gives him no answer. He disguises himself and visits a medium at Endor by night. He asks her to bring up Samuel. Samuel says the LORD has given the kingdom to David. Tomorrow Saul and his sons will die. Saul falls to the ground, and the woman persuades him to eat.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 1 Samuel names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The older manual says the speaker was not Samuel. The chapter itself repeatedly calls him Samuel. What danger does the woman name in verse 9?

contextNote.title: Saul seeks help from someone his policy endangered
contextNote.text: Saul comes for help to a person his own law condemned (verse 3). In verse 9 she fears the visit is a trap. Saul swears by the LORD that she will not be punished (verse 10). He uses God’s name to protect a practice God’s law forbids. The message he receives adds little to chapter 15 (verses 17–18). Only the date is new: tomorrow. The woman he endangered is the one who feeds him (verses 21–25).

passages.title: Philistine leaders send David away
passages.summary: The Philistine armies gather at Aphek, and David marches at the rear with Achish. The Philistine commanders ask what these Hebrews are doing there. Achish says he has found no fault in David. The commanders are angry and demand that David be sent back. They quote the song about Saul’s thousands and David’s ten thousands. Achish apologizes and tells David to leave at dawn. David protests that he has done nothing wrong. He and his men return south in the morning.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Why do the Philistine leaders distrust David, even though Achish trusts him?

contextNote.title: Suspicion prevents divided service in battle
contextNote.text: David’s lie to Achish has now trapped him. He must fight Israel or betray the king who sheltered him. The commanders’ suspicion in verse 4 opens a way out. They reason that Saul’s former officer could win back favor with Philistine heads. The old song follows David even here (verse 5). The text never says what David meant to do. His protest in verse 8 can be read either way.

passages.title: David recovers the captives and shares the spoil
passages.summary: David returns to Ziklag and finds it burned by Amalekites. The wives and children are gone, and his men talk of stoning him. David finds strength in the LORD and asks whether to pursue. Two hundred men are too tired to cross the brook Besor. An abandoned Egyptian slave leads the rest to the raiders. David recovers every person and all the goods. Some men want to give the two hundred nothing. David rules that all share alike and sends gifts to Judah’s elders.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Why does David share recovered goods with people who stayed behind?

contextNote.title: Recovery creates a dispute about who deserves a share
contextNote.text: Some of the four hundred claim the spoil as their own earnings (verse 22). David answers in verse 23 that the LORD gave it. A gift cannot be divided like wages. Verse 24 therefore gives the guards of the baggage an equal share. Verse 25 says this became a lasting rule in Israel. David also feeds a slave whose master left him to die (verses 11–12). The gifts in verse 26 reach the elders who will soon crown him.

passages.title: Saul and his sons die at Gilboa
passages.summary: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan and two of his brothers are killed. Archers wound Saul badly. He asks his armor bearer to kill him, and the man is afraid. Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor bearer does the same. The Philistines cut off Saul’s head and hang his body on Beth Shan’s wall. Men of Jabesh Gilead march all night and take the bodies down. They burn them, bury the bones, and fast seven days.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: How do the people of Jabesh Gilead honor Saul after his defeat?

contextNote.title: An earlier rescue returns as care for the dead
contextNote.text: Jabesh Gilead is the town Saul rescued in chapter 11. That rescue was his first act as king. Now its men cross the Jordan at night into enemy ground (verse 12). They take the bodies from a city wall. They bury the bones and fast (verse 13). The book gives no speech about Saul’s reign at his death. Its last scene of him is the gratitude of people he once saved.

events.title: Hannah prays and dedicates Samuel
events.summary: Elkanah has two wives, and Hannah has no children. Each year at Shiloh the other wife taunts her until she weeps. Hannah prays in bitter grief and vows to give a son to the LORD. Eli the priest sees her lips move and thinks she is drunk. She explains, and he sends her away with a blessing. She bears a son and names him Samuel. When he is weaned she brings him to Eli at Shiloh. She gives him to the LORD for his whole life.
events.detail: Three people misread Hannah in this chapter. Her rival provokes her (verse 6). Her husband asks if he is not better than ten sons (verse 8). The priest takes her silent prayer for drunkenness (verses 13–14). In verses 15–16 she corrects him firmly and with respect. Eli changes his charge into a blessing (verse 17). Verse 18 says her face was no longer sad, before any child is born.
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson studies Hannah's prayer during grief and her trust in God. How does Hannah answer Eli in verses 15–16?

events.title: Hannah’s song and the failure of Eli’s sons
events.summary: Hannah sings that the LORD brings down the strong and lifts the poor. Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are priests who do not know the LORD. They take the best meat by force before the fat is burned. They also sleep with women who serve at the tent door. Eli rebukes them, but they do not listen. Meanwhile the boy Samuel grows and serves before the LORD. A man of God tells Eli that his house will lose the priesthood. Both sons will die on one day.
events.detail: The sons’ sin is plain in verses 13–17 and 22. Eli’s part is harder to see. He does speak to them (verses 23–25), but with words only. Verse 29 charges him with honoring his sons above God. It also says “yourselves,” so he shares in what they took. Verse 30 states the rule that follows: the LORD honors those who honor him. Between these scenes the text keeps noting Samuel’s growth (verses 18, 21, 26).

lds.text: The older Church manual connects Hannah's song with Jesus Christ. What does the man of God say Eli has honored above the LORD (verse 29)?

events.title: Samuel hears the call
events.summary: The boy Samuel serves under Eli, and words from the LORD are rare. One night a voice calls Samuel, and he runs to Eli. This happens three times before Eli understands. He tells Samuel to answer, “Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.” The LORD says he will judge Eli’s house for the sons’ sin. Eli knew and did not restrain them. In the morning Samuel is afraid, but Eli makes him tell everything. All Israel learns that Samuel is a prophet.
events.detail: Samuel’s first message is a judgment on the man who raised him. Verse 15 says he was afraid to tell it. Eli himself taught the boy how to listen (verse 9). Eli also insists on hearing every word (verse 17). In verse 18 Samuel hides nothing, and Eli accepts the sentence. The text does not report that he changed anything afterward. Verse 19 says the LORD let none of Samuel’s words fail.
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Samuel’s response with learning to recognize revelation. Who teaches Samuel how to answer the voice (verses 8–9)?

events.title: The ark is captured and Eli’s household suffers loss
events.summary: Israel fights the Philistines and loses four thousand men. The elders send to Shiloh for the ark of the covenant. Hophni and Phinehas come with it, and the camp shouts. The Philistines are afraid but urge each other to fight like men. Israel loses thirty thousand men, the ark is captured, and Eli’s sons die. A runner brings the news to Shiloh. Eli falls from his seat and dies when he hears about the ark. His daughter-in-law dies in childbirth and names her son Ichabod.
events.detail: The elders ask a good question in verse 3: why did the LORD defeat us? They do not wait for an answer. They send for the ark so that “it” may save them. The priests who come with it are the two condemned in 2:34. The shout in verse 5 is confident, and the loss is far worse. Chapter 7:3–4 later shows what was missing here. The people had not put away their other gods.
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson examines trust in the ark. Why does carrying the ark fail to protect the army?

events.title: The ark among the Philistine towns
events.summary: The Philistines bring the ark to Ashdod and set it beside their god Dagon. The next morning Dagon’s statue lies face down before the ark. They set it up, and the next day it has fallen again. Its head and hands lie broken on the threshold. The LORD strikes Ashdod with tumors. The people send the ark to Gath, and the same thing happens. Gath sends it to Ekron, and Ekron cries out in terror. The city’s cry goes up to heaven.
events.detail: The Philistines won the battle and placed the ark as a trophy (verse 2). No Israelite soldier or priest is present in this chapter. The LORD acts alone in the enemy’s own temple. In verse 7 the men of Ashdod read the events correctly. His hand is heavy on them and on Dagon. Their answer is to send the problem to the next town (verse 8). Each move spreads the harm (verses 9–12).
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The older manual connects the ark’s troubles with Israel’s need to honor God. What do the men of Ashdod conclude in verse 7?

events.title: The ark returns to Beth Shemesh
events.summary: After seven months the Philistines ask their priests how to send the ark back. The priests advise a guilt offering of five golden tumors and five golden mice. They warn the people not to harden their hearts as Egypt did. They hitch two milk cows to a new cart and pen up the calves. If the cows go toward Israel, the LORD sent the plague. The cows walk straight to Beth Shemesh, lowing as they go. The people there rejoice and offer the cows. Some look into the ark and die, and the town sends it away.
events.detail: The Philistine priests design a test in verses 7–9. Nursing cows that never pulled a cart should turn back to their calves. If they leave, something stronger than instinct is moving them. Verse 9 names the other option honestly: it may have been chance. Verse 12 reports the result, with the cows lowing all the way. The ark is no safer for Israel’s own town (verse 19). Beth Shemesh asks who can stand before this holy God (verse 20).
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson uses these events to study trust and obedience. Why do the Philistines use cows that have calves at home (verses 7–9)?

events.title: Samuel leads the gathering at Mizpah
events.summary: The ark stays at Kiriath Jearim for twenty years. Samuel tells Israel to put away foreign gods and serve the LORD alone. They do so and gather at Mizpah to fast and confess. The Philistines hear of the gathering and attack. The people beg Samuel to keep praying for them. He offers a lamb, and the LORD thunders against the Philistines. Israel chases them, and Samuel sets up a stone named Ebenezer. Samuel judges Israel on a yearly circuit from his home in Ramah.
events.detail: The name Ebenezer first appears in 4:1, where Israel camped before defeat. There the people fetched the ark and shouted. Here they put away their gods and confess (verses 4 and 6). They ask Samuel to pray; they do not ask for an object (verse 8). The same enemy is driven back. In verse 12 Samuel marks the place with a stone and a name. His words are modest: the LORD has helped “until now.”
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies turning toward God after earlier failure. What does Israel do in verses 3–6 before the battle?

events.title: The people request a king
events.summary: Samuel grows old, and his sons take bribes as judges. The elders ask him for a king like all the nations have. Samuel is displeased and prays. The LORD says the people have rejected him, not Samuel, as king. Samuel must warn them how a king will behave. A king will take their sons, daughters, fields, crops, servants, and flocks. They will cry out, and the LORD will not answer. The people still insist, and the LORD tells Samuel to give them a king.
events.detail: The elders have a real complaint: Samuel’s sons are corrupt (verse 3). Their fix is to be “like all the nations” (verse 5). Samuel’s warning repeats one phrase again and again: “he will take.” The list runs from sons and daughters to fields and flocks (verses 11–17). Verse 17 ends it: “you will be his servants.” The LORD once brought Israel out of service to a king in Egypt. The people hear all this and still choose it (verses 19–20).
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and broad regions. Camp, cave, and house positions are not certain.

lds.text: The Church lesson invites readers to consider Jesus Christ as their King. What does verse 17 say the people will become under a king?

events.title: Saul searches for donkeys and meets Samuel
events.summary: Saul, a tall young man of Benjamin, searches for his father’s lost donkeys. After three days he wants to turn back. His servant suggests asking a man of God in the nearby town. The servant also supplies the silver for a gift. The day before, the LORD told Samuel that a Benjamite would come. Samuel must anoint him as leader over Israel. Samuel seats Saul at the head of a feast and gives him a reserved portion. Saul says his tribe is the smallest and his family the least.
events.detail: Saul is about to give up the search in verse 5. The unnamed servant knows about the man of God (verse 6). The servant also has the quarter shekel (verse 8). Saul does not even recognize Samuel at the gate (verse 18). Verses 15–16 show the other side of the story. The LORD had already told Samuel when the man would come. Lost donkeys and a servant’s idea bring Saul to that meeting.

events.title: Saul is anointed and presented publicly
events.summary: Samuel pours oil on Saul’s head and names three signs for the road home. All three happen, and God gives Saul another heart. The Spirit comes on him, and he prophesies among a band of prophets. He tells his uncle about the donkeys but not about the kingdom. Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah and chooses by lot. The lot falls on Saul, who is hiding among the baggage. The people shout, “Long live the king!” Some men despise him, and he keeps silent.
events.detail: Saul already has the oil, the signs, and a changed heart (verses 1–9). When the lot falls on him, he cannot be found. The people must ask the LORD where he is (verse 22). The text gives no reason for his hiding. It may be modesty or fear, and the chapter leaves that open. Samuel presents him by his height (verses 23–24). In verse 19 Samuel has just said that Israel rejected God that day.

events.title: Saul relieves Jabesh Gilead
events.summary: Nahash the Ammonite surrounds Jabesh Gilead. He will make peace only if he may put out every right eye. The town sends messengers through Israel. Saul comes in from the field behind his oxen and hears the news. God’s Spirit comes on him, and he is very angry. He cuts up the oxen and sends the pieces as a summons. Israel gathers, and Saul breaks the Ammonite camp at dawn. He refuses to punish his critics, and the people renew the kingdom at Gilgal.
events.detail: In 10:27 some men asked how Saul could save them. After the victory the people want those men put to death (verse 12). Saul now has the power and the public support to do it. Verse 13 records his refusal. He gives the credit for the rescue to the LORD, not to himself. This is Saul at his best: moved by the Spirit and restrained in victory. Later chapters should be read against this one.

events.title: Samuel reviews leadership and covenant responsibility
events.summary: Samuel speaks to all Israel now that a king leads them. He asks whom he has cheated, oppressed, or taken a bribe from. The people answer that he has taken nothing. He reviews how the LORD rescued them each time they cried out. Still they asked for a king when the LORD was their king. If they and their king obey, it will go well. Samuel calls for thunder and rain at wheat harvest, and the people are afraid. He promises to keep praying for them and teaching them.
events.detail: In 8:11–17 Samuel warned that a king would “take.” In verse 3 he asks whose ox or donkey he himself has taken. The people clear him before the LORD and the new king (verses 4–5). His clean record becomes the standard the king will be measured by. Verses 14–15 place king and people under the same condition. Samuel gives up rule but not his work. Verse 23 says he would sin if he stopped praying for them.

events.title: Pressure at Michmash and Saul’s offering
events.summary: Jonathan attacks a Philistine post, and the Philistines gather a huge army. Israel’s men hide in caves and pits, and some cross the Jordan. Saul waits seven days at Gilgal for Samuel, as he was told. Samuel does not come, and the soldiers begin to leave. Saul offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives at once and says Saul’s kingdom will not last. The LORD has sought a man after his own heart. Saul is left with six hundred men, and only he and Jonathan have swords.
events.detail: Saul’s answer in verse 11 lists three things he saw. The people were scattering, Samuel was late, and the Philistines had gathered. Verses 5–8 confirm that all three were true. His conclusion follows in verse 12: “I forced myself.” Every reason concerns what he could see. None concerns the instruction in 10:8 to wait. Samuel’s reply in verse 13 names only that: Saul did not keep the command.

events.title: Jonathan’s attack and Saul’s dangerous oath
events.summary: Jonathan and his armor bearer climb to a Philistine post alone. Jonathan says the LORD can save by many or by few. They kill about twenty men, and panic spreads through the Philistine camp. Saul joins the fight and puts a curse on anyone who eats before evening. Jonathan has not heard it and eats some honey. The hungry soldiers later eat meat with the blood. God gives Saul no answer, and the lot falls on Jonathan. Saul says he must die, but the people rescue him.
events.detail: Saul’s oath in verse 24 speaks of “my enemies.” It weakens his own army on the day of victory. Jonathan says so plainly in verse 29: his father has troubled the land. The hunger leads the soldiers to break the law about blood (verse 32). Saul then swears twice more that the guilty will die (verses 39 and 44). In verse 45 the people overrule their king. They say Jonathan worked “with God” that day.

events.title: Amalek, Agag, and Saul’s rejection
events.summary: Samuel gives Saul the LORD’s command to destroy Amalek completely. The reason given is Amalek’s attack on Israel after Egypt. Saul defeats them but spares King Agag and the best animals. The LORD tells Samuel he regrets making Saul king. Saul greets Samuel and claims he has obeyed. Samuel asks about the sheep he hears and says obeying is better than sacrifice. Saul admits he feared the people, and the LORD rejects him as king. Samuel kills Agag and never visits Saul again.
events.detail: Saul’s account changes as Samuel presses him. In verse 13 he says he has done what the LORD commanded. In verse 15 “they” spared the animals, for sacrifice. In verses 20–21 he obeyed, but “the people” took the plunder. Verse 9 had said that Saul and the people spared them together. He speaks of “the LORD your God” three times (verses 15, 21, 30). In verse 30 he still asks to be honored before the elders.

events.title: David is anointed and enters Saul’s service
events.summary: The LORD sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a son of Jesse. Samuel admires the eldest, but the LORD looks at the heart. Seven sons pass by, and none is chosen. The youngest, David, is brought from the sheep, and Samuel anoints him. The LORD’s Spirit comes on David and leaves Saul. A troubling spirit torments Saul, and his servants seek a harp player. One of them recommends David. David enters Saul’s service, and his music gives the king relief.
events.detail: In verses 13–14 the Spirit comes on David and leaves Saul. Saul’s own servants then bring the newly anointed man to court (verse 18). Saul loves him and makes him armor bearer (verse 21). He does not know what Samuel did in Bethlehem. David’s first service to the king is to ease him, not replace him. He plays a harp (verse 23); the Egyptian harp shown is only a comparison. The text says the troubling spirit was “from God” and explains no more.

events.title: David faces Goliath in the Valley of Elah
events.summary: The Philistine champion Goliath challenges Israel to single combat for forty days. Saul and his army are afraid. David brings food to his brothers and hears the challenge. He tells Saul that the LORD saved him from a lion and a bear. Saul dresses David in his own armor, but David takes it off. He chooses five smooth stones and his sling. He tells Goliath that the battle is the LORD’s. One stone sinks into the giant’s forehead, and David cuts off his head.
events.detail: Verses 5–7 list Goliath’s armor and weapons piece by piece. Saul answers in kind in verse 38 with a helmet and coat of mail. Saul is Israel’s tallest man (9:2) and its king, yet he stays back. David says he cannot go in gear he has not tested (verse 39). In verse 40 he takes a shepherd’s tools. His speech in verses 45–47 gives the reason. The LORD does not save by sword and spear.

events.title: Friendship, jealousy, and royal marriage plans
events.summary: Jonathan loves David and makes a covenant with him. He gives David his own robe, sword, and bow. Women sing that Saul has killed thousands and David ten thousands. Saul becomes angry and watches David from that day. Twice he throws a spear at him. He offers his daughter Merab, then gives her to another man. Michal loves David, and Saul asks a deadly bride price, hoping the Philistines kill him. David pays double, and Saul fears him even more.
events.detail: The song praises Saul too, but he hears only the comparison. In verse 8 he leaps from a song to the loss of his kingdom. Jonathan is the heir and has the most to lose. Yet in verse 4 he hands David his robe and weapons. The chapter repeats that the LORD was with David (verses 12, 14, 28). It also repeats that Saul was afraid (verses 12, 15, 29). Each plan to harm David ends by raising him higher.

events.title: Michal helps David escape
events.summary: Saul tells Jonathan and his servants to kill David. Jonathan defends David, and Saul swears he will not die. War returns, David wins again, and Saul throws his spear a third time. Saul’s men watch David’s house that night. Michal lowers David from a window and puts a household idol in his bed. David flees to Samuel at Ramah. Three groups of Saul’s messengers are overcome and begin to prophesy. Saul goes himself, and the Spirit overcomes him too.
events.detail: Both of Saul’s children protect David against him. Jonathan does it by argument (verses 4–5). Michal does it by a trick (verses 11–16). In verse 17 Saul calls her husband “my enemy.” Michal shields herself with a lie, and the text does not comment. Saul’s oath in verse 6 lasts only until the next spear (verse 10). In verses 23–24 the Spirit stops him when nothing else has.

events.title: Jonathan warns David and renews their covenant
events.summary: David asks Jonathan why Saul wants him dead. They agree on a test at the new moon feast. Jonathan asks David to show kindness to his family in the future. At the feast Saul notices David’s empty seat. He rages at Jonathan and says David blocks his way to the throne. Jonathan asks what David has done, and Saul throws a spear at him. Jonathan warns David with a signal of arrows in the field. They weep, swear friendship again, and part.
events.detail: Saul states the matter plainly in verse 31. While David lives, Jonathan will not be king. On the facts Saul is right, and Jonathan already knows it. In verses 14–15 he asks David to spare his family later. He speaks as if David’s rule is certain. His answer to his father in verse 32 is about justice. Saul’s reply is a spear thrown at his own son (verse 33).

events.title: David seeks food at Nob and refuge at Gath
events.summary: David flees alone to the priests at Nob. He tells Ahimelech that the king sent him on secret business. He asks for bread, and the priest has only the holy bread. Ahimelech gives it once he hears the men have kept from women. David also takes Goliath’s sword, which was kept there. Doeg the Edomite, Saul’s chief herdsman, is present that day. David goes on to King Achish of Gath, where the servants recognize him. He pretends to be mad, and Achish sends him away.
events.detail: Leviticus 24:5–9 reserves this bread for the priests. Ahimelech asks one question about the men’s condition (verse 4). Then he gives the bread, and verse 6 explains that no other was there. The text treats a hungry man’s need as reason enough. Jesus later cites this meal in Matthew 12:3–4. David gained the bread with a false story (verse 2). Verse 7 notes who was watching, and chapter 22 shows the cost.

events.title: David gathers followers and Saul orders the Nob massacre
events.summary: David hides in the cave of Adullam. His family and about four hundred troubled men join him. He leaves his parents with the king of Moab. Saul complains that his servants conspire against him. Doeg reports that Ahimelech gave David food and a sword. Ahimelech says David was the king’s loyal son-in-law. Saul orders the priests killed, and only Doeg obeys. Eighty-five priests and the town of Nob die, and Abiathar escapes to David.
events.detail: Saul’s order in verse 17 names the victims as “priests of the LORD.” His own guards hear those words and will not strike. Their refusal is silent, and the text records no punishment. Doeg, a foreigner, does what Israelites refuse to do (verse 18). Verse 19 lists men, women, children, and animals. Saul spared such things in Amalek against a command (15:9). David admits in verse 22 that his visit caused these deaths.

events.title: Keilah, wilderness pursuit, and Jonathan’s support
events.summary: David asks the LORD twice and then rescues the town of Keilah from Philistines. Saul hears and prepares to trap him inside its gates. David asks through the priest’s ephod whether Keilah will hand him over. The answer is yes, so he leaves with six hundred men. Jonathan finds him in the wilderness and strengthens his trust in God. The people of Ziph tell Saul where David hides. Saul closes in around a mountain. A Philistine raid calls him away just in time.
events.detail: David has just saved Keilah from its enemies (verse 5). Verse 12 says the town would still give him to Saul. The text gives no reason. The fate of Nob in 22:19 was recent, and Keilah had walls to lose. David does not punish or argue; he leaves (verse 13). Saul assumes God has handed David to him (verse 7). David asks instead of assuming, and the answer keeps him alive.

events.title: David spares Saul in the cave
events.summary: Saul takes three thousand men to hunt David at En Gedi. He enters a cave alone, and David’s men are hiding deep inside. They say the LORD has given David his enemy. David cuts off a corner of Saul’s robe and then regrets even that. He will not harm the LORD’s anointed. Outside, he bows and shows Saul the cloth. Saul weeps and says David is more righteous than he is. He admits David will be king and asks mercy for his family.
events.detail: David’s men and David read the same chance in opposite ways. They see a gift from God (verse 4). He sees a king whom God anointed (verse 6). In verse 11 the piece of robe serves as evidence. He could have killed, and the cloth shows he chose not to. He calls Saul “my father” and leaves judgment to the LORD (verse 12). Saul agrees with every word, yet verse 22 has them go separate ways.

events.title: Abigail prevents David’s revenge
events.summary: Samuel dies, and Israel mourns him. David’s men have guarded the flocks of Nabal, a rich and harsh man. David asks for food at shearing time, and Nabal insults him. David arms four hundred men and swears to kill every male. Nabal’s wife Abigail hurries out with food and meets David on the road. She asks him not to shed blood he will later regret. David blesses her and turns back. Nabal dies ten days later, and David marries Abigail.
events.detail: In chapter 24 David spared a king who hunted him. Here an insult is enough to send him out with swords (verses 21–22). Abigail acts without telling her husband (verse 19). Her case in verses 30–31 looks ahead to David’s rule. A future king should not carry needless bloodshed on his conscience. In verse 33 David admits she stopped him from avenging himself. He credits the LORD with sending her (verse 32).

events.title: David takes the spear and water jar
events.summary: The people of Ziph again tell Saul where David is. Saul camps with three thousand men. David and Abishai slip into the camp at night and find Saul asleep. Abishai offers to pin him to the ground with one stroke. David forbids it and takes Saul’s spear and water jar. From a far hill he calls to Abner and to Saul. Saul admits he has played the fool and promises no more harm. David returns the spear, and each goes his own way.
events.detail: David’s words in verse 16 are aimed at Abner, the king’s guard. The missing spear and jar prove how close death came. Saul threw that spear at David in 18:11 and 19:10. David has it in his hand and sends it back (verse 22). His reason is in verses 10–11: the LORD will deal with Saul. Saul’s blessing in verse 25 sounds like peace. In 27:1 David still expects Saul to kill him.

events.title: David lives under Achish and conceals his raids
events.summary: David decides that Saul will one day kill him. He crosses to the Philistines with six hundred men and their families. King Achish of Gath gives him the town of Ziklag. Saul stops searching for him. David raids the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites to the south. He leaves no one alive and takes the livestock. He tells Achish that he has raided Judah. Achish believes David’s own people now hate him.
events.detail: Verse 11 states David’s reason in plain terms. He leaves no one alive who could report to Gath. The chapter does not say the LORD ordered these raids. David asked the LORD before acting in 23:2 and 23:4. No such question appears here. His safety with Achish rests on a lie (verse 10). Verse 12 shows that Achish is fully deceived.

events.title: Saul consults the woman at Endor
events.summary: The Philistines gather for war, and Achish expects David to fight for him. Samuel is dead, and Saul has driven mediums from the land. Saul is afraid, and the LORD gives him no answer. He disguises himself and visits a medium at Endor by night. He asks her to bring up Samuel. Samuel says the LORD has given the kingdom to David. Tomorrow Saul and his sons will die. Saul falls to the ground, and the woman persuades him to eat.
events.detail: Saul comes for help to a person his own law condemned (verse 3). In verse 9 she fears the visit is a trap. Saul swears by the LORD that she will not be punished (verse 10). He uses God’s name to protect a practice God’s law forbids. The message he receives adds little to chapter 15 (verses 17–18). Only the date is new: tomorrow. The woman he endangered is the one who feeds him (verses 21–25).

events.title: Philistine leaders send David away
events.summary: The Philistine armies gather at Aphek, and David marches at the rear with Achish. The Philistine commanders ask what these Hebrews are doing there. Achish says he has found no fault in David. The commanders are angry and demand that David be sent back. They quote the song about Saul’s thousands and David’s ten thousands. Achish apologizes and tells David to leave at dawn. David protests that he has done nothing wrong. He and his men return south in the morning.
events.detail: David’s lie to Achish has now trapped him. He must fight Israel or betray the king who sheltered him. The commanders’ suspicion in verse 4 opens a way out. They reason that Saul’s former officer could win back favor with Philistine heads. The old song follows David even here (verse 5). The text never says what David meant to do. His protest in verse 8 can be read either way.

events.title: David recovers the captives and shares the spoil
events.summary: David returns to Ziklag and finds it burned by Amalekites. The wives and children are gone, and his men talk of stoning him. David finds strength in the LORD and asks whether to pursue. Two hundred men are too tired to cross the brook Besor. An abandoned Egyptian slave leads the rest to the raiders. David recovers every person and all the goods. Some men want to give the two hundred nothing. David rules that all share alike and sends gifts to Judah’s elders.
events.detail: Some of the four hundred claim the spoil as their own earnings (verse 22). David answers in verse 23 that the LORD gave it. A gift cannot be divided like wages. Verse 24 therefore gives the guards of the baggage an equal share. Verse 25 says this became a lasting rule in Israel. David also feeds a slave whose master left him to die (verses 11–12). The gifts in verse 26 reach the elders who will soon crown him.

events.title: Saul and his sons die at Gilboa
events.summary: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan and two of his brothers are killed. Archers wound Saul badly. He asks his armor bearer to kill him, and the man is afraid. Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor bearer does the same. The Philistines cut off Saul’s head and hang his body on Beth Shan’s wall. Men of Jabesh Gilead march all night and take the bodies down. They burn them, bury the bones, and fast seven days.
events.detail: Jabesh Gilead is the town Saul rescued in chapter 11. That rescue was his first act as king. Now its men cross the Jordan at night into enemy ground (verse 12). They take the bodies from a city wall. They bury the bones and fast (verse 13). The book gives no speech about Saul’s reign at his death. Its last scene of him is the gratitude of people he once saved.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Ammon · approximate

regions.name: Moab · approximate

guides.title: 1 Samuel: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A king can take what a people needs
steps.text: The elders have a real complaint: Samuel’s sons are corrupt (verse 3). Their fix is to be “like all the nations” (verse 5). Samuel’s warning repeats one phrase again and again: “he will take.” The list runs from sons and daughters to fields and flocks (verses 11–17). Verse 17 ends it: “you will be his servants.” The LORD once brought Israel out of service to a king in Egypt. The people hear all this and still choose it (verses 19–20).

steps.title: Music belongs inside the court
steps.text: In verses 13–14 the Spirit comes on David and leaves Saul. Saul’s own servants then bring the newly anointed man to court (verse 18). Saul loves him and makes him armor bearer (verse 21). He does not know what Samuel did in Bethlehem. David’s first service to the king is to ease him, not replace him. He plays a harp (verse 23); the Egyptian harp shown is only a comparison. The text says the troubling spirit was “from God” and explains no more.

steps.title: Wisdom stops violence before it gains praise
steps.text: In chapter 24 David spared a king who hunted him. Here an insult is enough to send him out with swords (verses 21–22). Abigail acts without telling her husband (verse 19). Her case in verses 30–31 looks ahead to David’s rule. A future king should not carry needless bloodshed on his conscience. In verse 33 David admits she stopped him from avenging himself. He credits the LORD with sending her (verse 32).

textRoutes.title: Hannah prays and dedicates Samuel
textRoutes.summary: Elkanah has two wives, and Hannah has no children. Each year at Shiloh the other wife taunts her until she weeps. Hannah prays in bitter grief and vows to give a son to the LORD. Eli the priest sees her lips move and thinks she is drunk. She explains, and he sends her away with a blessing. She bears a son and names him Samuel. When he is weaned she brings him to Eli at Shiloh. She gives him to the LORD for his whole life.
textRoutes.detail: Three people misread Hannah in this chapter. Her rival provokes her (verse 6). Her husband asks if he is not better than ten sons (verse 8). The priest takes her silent prayer for drunkenness (verses 13–14). In verses 15–16 she corrects him firmly and with respect. Eli changes his charge into a blessing (verse 17). Verse 18 says her face was no longer sad, before any child is born.

textRoutes.title: The ark is captured and Eli’s household suffers loss
textRoutes.summary: Israel fights the Philistines and loses four thousand men. The elders send to Shiloh for the ark of the covenant. Hophni and Phinehas come with it, and the camp shouts. The Philistines are afraid but urge each other to fight like men. Israel loses thirty thousand men, the ark is captured, and Eli’s sons die. A runner brings the news to Shiloh. Eli falls from his seat and dies when he hears about the ark. His daughter-in-law dies in childbirth and names her son Ichabod.
textRoutes.detail: The elders ask a good question in verse 3: why did the LORD defeat us? They do not wait for an answer. They send for the ark so that “it” may save them. The priests who come with it are the two condemned in 2:34. The shout in verse 5 is confident, and the loss is far worse. Chapter 7:3–4 later shows what was missing here. The people had not put away their other gods.

In verse 7 the men of Ashdod read the events correctly. His hand is heavy on them and on Dagon. Their answer is to send the problem to the next town (verse 8). Each move spreads the harm (verses 9–12).

textRoutes.title: Samuel leads the gathering at Mizpah
textRoutes.summary: The ark stays at Kiriath Jearim for twenty years. Samuel tells Israel to put away foreign gods and serve the LORD alone. They do so and gather at Mizpah to fast and confess. The Philistines hear of the gathering and attack. The people beg Samuel to keep praying for them. He offers a lamb, and the LORD thunders against the Philistines. textRoutes.title: Saul relieves Jabesh Gilead

textRoutes.title: David is anointed and enters Saul’s service
textRoutes.summary: The LORD sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a son of Jesse. Samuel admires the eldest, but the LORD looks at the heart. Seven sons pass by, and none is chosen. The youngest, David, is brought from the sheep, and Samuel anoints him. The LORD’s Spirit comes on David and leaves Saul. A troubling spirit torments Saul, and his servants seek a harp player. textRoutes.title: David faces Goliath in the Valley of Elah
textRoutes.summary: The Philistine champion Goliath challenges Israel to single combat for forty days. Saul and his army are afraid. David brings food to his brothers and hears the challenge. He tells Saul that the LORD saved him from a lion and a bear. Saul dresses David in his own armor, but David takes it off. He chooses five smooth stones and his sling. textRoutes.title: Michal helps David escape

textRoutes.title: David seeks food at Nob and refuge at Gath

textRoutes.title: Keilah, wilderness pursuit, and Jonathan’s support
textRoutes.summary: David asks the LORD twice and then rescues the town of Keilah from Philistines. Saul hears and prepares to trap him inside its gates. textRoutes.summary: David decides that Saul will one day kill him. He crosses to the Philistines with six hundred men and their families. King Achish of Gath gives him the town of Ziklag. textRoutes.title: Philistine leaders send David away
textRoutes.summary: The Philistine armies gather at Aphek, and David marches at the rear with Achish. The Philistine commanders ask what these Hebrews are doing there. Achish says he has found no fault in David. The commanders are angry and demand that David be sent back. They quote the song about Saul’s thousands and David’s ten thousands. textRoutes.title: David recovers the captives and shares the spoil
textRoutes.summary: David returns to Ziklag and finds it burned by Amalekites. The wives and children are gone, and his men talk of stoning him. textRoutes.title: Saul and his sons die at Gilboa
textRoutes.summary: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan and two of his brothers are killed. Archers wound Saul badly. He asks his armor bearer to kill him, and the man is afraid.
